items.prompt: What does `git push --force` actually do?
choices: Replaces whatever the remote branch currently points to with whatever the local branch currently points to, discarding remote commits not reachable from the new local tip
Merges the local and remote branches automatically, keeping all commits from both
Creates a backup of the remote branch before pushing any changes
Sends an email notification to every collaborator before pushing
items.explanation: Force-push unconditionally overwrites the remote ref — it doesn't merge, back up, or notify anyone by itself.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what did the developer's force-push actually overwrite?
choices: The remote branch's pointer, moving it from the teammate's already-pushed commit to the developer's rebased commit
The teammate's local repository on their own machine
The company's entire git server configuration
Nothing — force-push only affects the pusher's own local branch
items.explanation: Force-push moves the remote branch's ref — it doesn't touch the teammate's local machine or server config, and it very much does affect the remote.

items.prompt: What is "shared history" in this unit's sense?
choices: Commit history on a branch that more than one person pushes to or bases work on
The complete commit log of every repository a company has ever created
A branch that's been merged into main at least once
The commits made during a pair-programming session specifically
items.explanation: Shared history is specifically about multiple people depending on the same branch's commits — not about total repo count, merge status, or pairing sessions.

items.prompt: Why does force-pushing become genuinely risky specifically on shared history?
choices: Because someone else may have already pushed commits based on the branch's current state, which a force-push can silently discard
Because git technically forbids force-pushing to any branch with more than one contributor
Because shared branches always have slower push speeds than personal branches
Force-pushing is never actually risky, regardless of who else uses the branch
items.explanation: The risk comes specifically from other people's dependent work being discardable — not a git restriction, speed issue, or absence of real risk.

items.prompt: What does it mean for commit A to be an "ancestor" of commit B?
choices: B's history, traced backward through parent commits, eventually reaches A
A was created before B chronologically, regardless of branch structure
A and B were both authored by the same person
A and B have identical file contents
items.explanation: Ancestry is specifically about reachability through the parent-commit chain — not creation time, authorship, or file content similarity.

items.prompt: A normal (non-force) push checks whether the remote's current tip is an ancestor of what's being pushed. Why does this check matter?
choices: If the remote's tip is an ancestor of the new commit, nothing on the remote would be lost by the push, so it's safe to proceed
This check only exists to speed up the push, with no safety implication at all
This check verifies the pusher has the correct file permissions
This check confirms the commit messages follow the team's style guide
items.explanation: The ancestor check is precisely git's built-in guarantee that a normal push can't discard commits — a permissions or style check would be unrelated to this specific mechanism.

items.prompt: What does `--force-with-lease` do differently from plain `--force`?
choices: It fails if the remote branch has moved since the last fetch, instead of silently overwriting whatever is there
It automatically merges conflicting commits instead of overwriting them
It requires a second team member to approve the push before it happens
It only works on branches with fewer than 10 commits
items.explanation: The defining difference is the check against the remote's actual current state — not automatic merging, approval workflows, or a commit-count limit.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, would `--force-with-lease` have prevented the teammate's commit from being lost?
choices: Yes — it would have detected that the remote had moved since the developer's last fetch and rejected the push
No — `--force-with-lease` behaves identically to plain `--force` in every case
Yes, but only if the teammate had also used `--force-with-lease` for their own push
No — `--force-with-lease` only works for pulling, never for pushing
items.explanation: The whole point of `--force-with-lease` is to catch exactly this situation — a remote that moved since the pusher's last known view of it.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, did the developer directly modify or delete the teammate's commit?
choices: No — the developer only rebased their own commits; the teammate's commit was lost as a side effect of the subsequent force-push
Yes — the developer explicitly ran a command to delete the teammate's specific commit
Yes — the developer edited the teammate's commit message before pushing
It's impossible to tell from the Scenario's facts what the developer actually did
items.explanation: The Scenario is explicit that the developer only touched their own commits — the loss was a side effect of the force-push overwriting the remote ref, not a direct action against the teammate's commit.

items.prompt: Why did the force-push in the Scenario produce no error or warning?
choices: Force-push explicitly skips the safety check a normal push performs, so there was nothing to catch the problem
Git always displays a warning before any force-push, but the developer ignored it
The teammate's commit had already been automatically backed up elsewhere, so git considered it safe
Force-push only produces warnings when used on branches named "main" specifically
items.explanation: Force explicitly bypasses the ancestor check a normal push relies on — there's no built-in warning step it goes through instead.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what happens when a normal (non-force) push finds that the remote's tip is NOT an ancestor of what's being pushed?
choices: The push is rejected, typically with a message prompting the pusher to fetch first
The push proceeds anyway, silently discarding the remote's extra commits
Git automatically force-pushes on the pusher's behalf without asking
The push succeeds but creates a duplicate branch with a different name
items.explanation: L2's diagram shows a normal push is rejected rather than proceeding or silently overwriting — that rejection is the safety mechanism working as intended.

items.prompt: Per L2, is rewriting your own not-yet-shared commit history (like squashing commits before anyone else sees them) inherently dangerous?
choices: No — it's described as a completely normal, safe operation; the danger only appears once someone else has already based work on the commits being rewritten
Yes — any rewriting of commit history is described as inherently dangerous under all circumstances
No, but only if the rewritten commits are less than one hour old
Yes, but only for repositories with more than 50 contributors
items.explanation: L2 explicitly distinguishes safe personal-history rewriting from the danger that appears once other people depend on those commits.

items.prompt: Per L2, what is a branch, mechanically, on the remote?
choices: A named pointer to one specific commit (its "tip")
A complete, separate copy of every commit in the repository
A folder on disk containing all the files changed in that branch
A permission setting controlling who can view the repository
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that a branch is just a pointer to a commit — not a full copy, a folder, or a permission setting.

items.prompt: Per L2, is a commit that's no longer reachable from any branch pointer immediately, permanently deleted?
choices: Not necessarily — it may still exist as an object in the repository for a while, but nothing points to it and nobody browsing the branch will see it
Yes — an unreachable commit is instantly and permanently erased from the repository the moment the ref moves
No — unreachable commits automatically become a new branch
Yes, but only if the repository has garbage collection disabled
items.explanation: L2 explicitly notes the commit object can persist for a while even when nothing points to it — 'gone from the branch's perspective' isn't the same as 'immediately erased.'

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with treating "I only rebased my own commits" as proof nothing else could be affected?
choices: The rebase itself only touches the rebaser's commits, but the force-push that follows can still discard someone else's commits if the remote moved in the meantime
Nothing is wrong with this reasoning — rebasing your own commits guarantees complete safety
This reasoning is wrong only when working on a branch with an odd number of commits
This reasoning is wrong only because rebasing is always slower than merging
items.explanation: L2 explicitly separates the rebase step (safe, self-contained) from the force-push step (where the actual risk to others' work lives).

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of force-pushing to a shared branch out of habit built on personal branches?
choices: A workflow that's perfectly safe on a branch nobody else touches becomes genuinely dangerous the moment that branch is shared, without the command itself looking any different
There's no real risk — force-push behaves identically regardless of how many people use a branch
The risk is purely about push speed, not about losing any commits
This risk only applies to branches with names longer than 20 characters
items.explanation: L2 highlights that the command's danger depends entirely on the branch's shared status, which the command syntax itself gives no indication of.

items.prompt: Implement commitsLostByForcePush and isAncestor so they correctly determine which commits a force-push would discard, using reachability from each commit's parent chain.

tests.description: the teammate's commit D is reported as lost when force-pushing E over it
tests.expr: expect(commitsLostByForcePush([{ hash: "A", parent: null }, { hash: "B", parent: "A" }, { hash: "C", parent: "B" }, { hash: "D", parent: "C" }, { hash: "E", parent: "C" }], "D", "E")).toEqual(["D"])

tests.description: D is not an ancestor of E, since E's chain never passes through D
tests.expr: expect(isAncestor([{ hash: "A", parent: null }, { hash: "B", parent: "A" }, { hash: "C", parent: "B" }, { hash: "D", parent: "C" }, { hash: "E", parent: "C" }], "D", "E")).toBe(false)

tests.description: C is an ancestor of E
tests.expr: expect(isAncestor([{ hash: "A", parent: null }, { hash: "B", parent: "A" }, { hash: "C", parent: "B" }, { hash: "D", parent: "C" }, { hash: "E", parent: "C" }], "C", "E")).toBe(true)

items.explanation: Walking backward from each tip through parent pointers gives the exact set of commits reachable from it — comparing the old remote tip's reachable set against the new local tip's reachable set gives precisely which commits a force-push would discard, which is the same walk isAncestor uses to check a single specific commit.
items.reference:
🔗 Reachability — walk backward through parent pointers from a tip
➖ Lost commits — reachable from the old tip, not reachable from the new one

Why: this is the exact calculation git's own ancestor check performs before allowing a normal push.

items.prompt: Implement commitsLostByForcePush and isAncestor so they correctly determine which commits a force-push would discard, using reachability from each commit's parent chain.

tests.description: the teammate's commit Y is reported as lost when force-pushing Z over it
tests.expr: expect(commitsLostByForcePush([{ hash: "X1", parent: null }, { hash: "X2", parent: "X1" }, { hash: "X3", parent: "X2" }, { hash: "Y", parent: "X3" }, { hash: "Z", parent: "X3" }], "Y", "Z")).toEqual(["Y"])

tests.description: Y is not an ancestor of Z, since Z's chain never passes through Y
tests.expr: expect(isAncestor([{ hash: "X1", parent: null }, { hash: "X2", parent: "X1" }, { hash: "X3", parent: "X2" }, { hash: "Y", parent: "X3" }, { hash: "Z", parent: "X3" }], "Y", "Z")).toBe(false)

tests.description: X3 is an ancestor of Z
tests.expr: expect(isAncestor([{ hash: "X1", parent: null }, { hash: "X2", parent: "X1" }, { hash: "X3", parent: "X2" }, { hash: "Y", parent: "X3" }, { hash: "Z", parent: "X3" }], "X3", "Z")).toBe(true)

items.explanation: Same calculation regardless of the commit names used: reachable-set comparison identifies exactly which commits a force-push would discard, and isAncestor performs the same backward walk to answer a single-commit version of the same question.
items.reference:
🔗 Reachability — walk backward through parent pointers from a tip
➖ Lost commits — reachable from the old tip, not reachable from the new one

Why: this is the exact calculation git's own ancestor check performs before allowing a normal push.

items.prompt: Implement forceWithLease so it rejects the push if the actual remote tip doesn't match the pusher's expected remote tip, and only updates the ref when they match.

tests.description: rejects the push when the remote has moved since the pusher's last known view
succeeds and updates the tip when the expectation matches the actual remote
does not mutate the branch name when updating the tip

items.explanation: Comparing the actual remote tip against what the pusher expected it to be (from their last fetch) is exactly what catches a remote that moved since then — a plain force-push never performs this comparison at all.
items.reference:
❌ Mismatch — remote moved since last fetch, push rejected
✅ Match — remote is exactly as expected, push proceeds

Why: this one comparison is the entire difference between a safe rewrite and a silent, destructive overwrite.

items.explanation: Same check regardless of the branch name or commit hashes used: comparing the actual remote tip against the pusher's expected tip is what catches a remote that moved since the last fetch.
